'''Paul Kuykendall Dayton''' (born April 8, 1941 in [[Tucson, Arizona]]) is a biological [[oceanographer]] and marine [[ecologist]] at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]]. Dayton works in [[Benthic zone|benthic]] ecology, marine conservation, evolution, natural history, and general ecology.

During a 35-year career at Scripps, Dayton has researched coastal [[Antarctic]] habitats and the rocky shore habitats of [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]] in order to better understand marine [[ecosystem]]s. He has also documented the environmental impacts of overfishing, and phenomena such as [[El Niño]] on coastal ecology.<ref name="prize">{{Cite web|title=News|url=https://scripps.ucsd.edu/news|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Scripps Institution of Oceanography|language=en}}</ref>

Dayton is the only person to win both the George Mercer Award (1974) and the WS Cooper Award (2000) from the [[Ecological Society of America]].{{Cn|date=July 2022}} In 2002, he received the Scientific Diving Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Academy of Underwater Sciences; in 2004 he was honored with the [[Edward O. Wilson Naturalist Award]] from the [[American Society of Naturalists]], and in 2006 was the first recipient of the [[Ramon Margalef Prize in Ecology]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=2005. Paul Dayton|url=http://presidencia.gencat.cat/en/detalls/Article/2005-Paul-Dayton|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Ministry of the Presidency|language=en-GB}}</ref> Dayton has been director of [[The Ocean Conservancy]] and the National Research Council Panel on Marine Protected Areas.<ref name="prize"/> He has been a frequent contributor to [[Science (journal)|''Science'']] magazine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Search Science|url=https://www.science.org/search/advanced?session_query_ref=rbs.queryref_1217945274298&COLLECTIONS=hw1&JC=sci&FULLTEXT=%28paul%20AND%20k%20AND%20dayton%29&FULLTEXTFIELD=lemcontent&RESOURCETYPE=HWCIT&ABSTRACTFIELD=lemhwcompabstract&TITLEFIELD=lemhwcomptitle|access-date=2021-03-28|website=search.sciencemag.org}}</ref>

Dayton's 1971 paper titled "Competition, disturbance and community organization: The provision and subsequent utilization of space in a rocky intertidal community" in ''[[Ecological Monographs]]''<ref name= "Dayton1971">{{cite journal|last1= Dayton|first1=P. K.|title= Competition, Disturbance, and Community Organization: The Provision and Subsequent Utilization of Space in a Rocky Intertidal Community|journal= Ecological Monographs|volume= 41|issue= 4|year= 1971|pages= 351–389|doi= 10.2307/1948498|jstor=1948498}}</ref> has been cited over 1800 times as of {{As of|2012|04|pre=|bare=yes}}.<ref>{{Cite web|title=info|url=http://apps.isiknowledge.com/full_record.do?product=UA&search_mode=GeneralSearch&qid=5&SID=4E@FJpCeEhk4Neeog@3&page=1&doc=1&colname=WOS%5B%5D}}</ref>

==Education==
Dayton received a [[Bachelor of Science]] from the [[University of Arizona]], [[Tucson]], in 1963. He then earned a doctorate in [[zoology]] at the [[University of Washington]] under [[Robert T. Paine (zoologist)|Robert T. Paine]], known for the [[Keystone species]] concept.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dayton {{!}} Curriculum Vitae|url=http://daytonlab.ucsd.edu/PKD/CV.htm|access-date=2021-03-28|website=daytonlab.ucsd.edu}}</ref>
